metadata.title: How Chinese Taipei used TIMSS data to reform mathematics education

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This brief is a policy narrative that summarizes TIMSS 2003 and TIMSS 2011 benchmark results (including international benchmark categories and reported attitudes) for Chinese Taipei and four other East Asian systems. It does not provide an analytic microdata workflow (e.g., IDB Analyzer outputs, weight variable names, or replicate-weight procedures), so the specific application of TIMSS complex-sampling weights cannot be verified from the text. The tables appear to report published TIMSS percentages and country mean mathematics scores with standard errors, which are typically derived from TIMSS scaling and sampling procedures. For any re-analysis using TIMSS microdata, analysts should apply the official TIMSS student/sampling weights and replicate weights supplied with the international database to obtain correct standard errors under the complex design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The document is not an empirical student-level modeling study; it reports descriptive policy-relevant TIMSS results (benchmark-category percentages and attitude percentages) and describes program implementation (After Class Support and Just Do Math). Because no PV-based achievement modeling is performed in this brief, plausible-value handling is not applicable to the presented analysis. Missing-data handling is therefore not documented for an ML/estimation pipeline in this brief, which is a reporting gap relative to an empirical modeling paper but consistent with the brief’s descriptive-policy purpose.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used published TIMSS 2003 and TIMSS 2011 results for the specified five East Asian systems (Chinese Taipei, Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, South Korea) at 4th and 8th grade mathematics. The brief does not describe any additional student-level inclusion/exclusion criteria or analytic subsample restrictions beyond the use of the TIMSS-reported benchmark categories and attitude indicators.

data.outcome_summary: This IEA Compass brief explains how Chinese Taipei used successive TIMSS cycles as an evidence base for mathematics education reform rather than presenting a new ML model. It highlights TIMSS 2003 findings for 4th and 8th grade mathematics, including a higher share of students in the “Below Intermediate” benchmark group and a larger-than-international-average percentage of students reporting low confidence and low enjoyment of mathematics. It then summarizes TIMSS 2011 changes: a small decline in the “below intermediate” group, but persistent gaps relative to other East Asian systems, alongside increases in low-confidence reporting and continued low enjoyment at 8th grade. The brief links these trends to policy actions: the 2006 After Class Support program (out-of-school supplementary courses) and the 2014 Just Do Math program (grounding activity modules, camps, and teacher professional development). It concludes that TIMSS results can guide monitoring of whether reforms improve both achievement and students’ motivation, while noting that the brief itself does not provide causal evaluation metrics or a modeling methodology.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is a policy brief that synthesizes previously published TIMSS and PISA results and describes program implementation; it does not conduct an original student-level predictive/causal analysis. As a result, there is no reported ML algorithm, no analytic sample size, no PV-handling or missing-data strategy for an estimation pipeline, and no model performance metrics to extract. The extraction therefore focuses on the described use of TIMSS benchmark and attitude indicators to inform education policy shifts.
